title: Quotations and citations
learningObjectives: Choose blockquote and q according to the length and context of quoted material.
Distinguish the cite element, the cite attribute, and an ordinary source link.
Preserve quotation wording and provide enough attribution for readers to locate the source.
Explain why quotation marks alone do not provide semantic structure or attribution.
Inspect the rendered quotation and verify that the markup remains meaningful without default browser styling.

understand.concept: HTML provides distinct semantics for quoted material. Use blockquote for a quotation presented as a separate block and q for a short quotation embedded in a sentence. The cite element identifies the title of a creative work (for example, a book, article, film, or report); it is not a complete citation record and should not be used as a generic wrapper for an author's name. The cite attribute on blockquote or q can provide a URL for the source, but browsers do not normally display that URL as visible attribution. Add a visible source link or attribution text when readers need to find the source.
understand.whyItMatters: Correct quotation semantics help assistive technology and future maintainers understand which words are quoted. Visible attribution supports verification and responsible reuse. Semantic markup does not itself establish copyright permission, academic citation compliance, or factual accuracy; those require appropriate source handling outside the HTML element choice.
understand.analogy: Think of a quotation as a passage in a report: the quoted passage is visually separated, while a source note tells the reader where it came from. HTML provides semantic elements for the passage, but you still have to supply a useful source note.
understand.analogyLimit: A browser's default indentation or quotation marks are presentation details and can be changed by CSS or user-agent styles. The element's meaning comes from the markup, not from how it happens to look.

explain.narrative: Choose the element from the role of the content, not from the appearance you want. A blockquote represents a longer quotation that forms its own block. A q element represents a short inline quotation; browsers commonly add quotation marks, but exact punctuation and styling can vary. Use cite for the title of the work being referenced. Use a normal a element for a source URL. If a quote is translated, shortened, or adapted, make that change clear in the surrounding attribution rather than implying that the wording is an exact quotation. Do not put quotation marks around ordinary text just to make it look important, and do not use blockquote merely to indent content.

examples.code:
Well-structured information is easier to understand and maintain.

— From Example Research Report, read the source.
examples.explanation: The blockquote contains the quoted passage. Its cite attribute records a source URL for machine-readable context, while the visible link lets a reader open the source. The cite element marks the title of the report, not the URL or the author's name.
examples.expectedOutput: A separate quotation block followed by a visible attribution and source link. Default indentation may vary by browser and stylesheet.

examples.code: The guide describes semantic HTML as meaning before appearance, then explains the idea in detail.
examples.explanation: The q element marks a short inline quotation within the sentence. Browsers generally provide quotation marks automatically; do not add duplicate quotation marks unless the content genuinely requires them.
examples.expectedOutput: One paragraph containing a short inline quotation. The browser may supply quotation marks according to its language and style rules.

examples.code: We reviewed HTML: The Living Standard before writing this section.
examples.explanation: cite identifies the title of a creative work. It is not the correct semantic element for a person's name, a generic source URL, or every bibliographic detail.
examples.expectedOutput: A paragraph with the work title marked as a citation title; its default visual style is not the semantic meaning.

examples.code:
Quoted words belong in a quotation element.

Source: Original source. The quotation was shortened for this example.
examples.explanation: The source link is visible and the surrounding text explains an editorial change. In a real lesson or publication, replace the example URL with the actual source and follow the required citation style.
examples.expectedOutput: A block quotation followed by a visible source link and a note about the shortened wording.

examples.code: Readable content should retain its meaning when styles are disabled.
examples.explanation: CSS changes the visual presentation without changing the quotation's semantic role. Removing the style block leaves meaningful HTML.
examples.expectedOutput: A visually emphasized quotation. The blockquote remains semantically meaningful if the CSS is removed.

practise.guidedTask: Create a page containing one block quotation and one inline quotation. Add a visible source link for each. Use cite only for the title of the referenced work. Then disable CSS and check whether the structure and attribution still make sense.
practise.independentTask: Prepare a short research note with two quotations from sources you are permitted to use. Preserve exact wording, identify any omissions or adaptations, provide visible source links, and use blockquote or q appropriately. Explain why the cite element is not a replacement for a full bibliography or required citation style.
hints: Use blockquote when the quoted material is a separate block; do not choose it merely to create indentation.
Use q for a short quotation inside a sentence; avoid adding duplicate quotation marks blindly.
The cite element identifies a work title. A person's name normally remains ordinary text unless another semantic element is appropriate.
The cite attribute is not a visible source note. Add a readable link or attribution when needed.
Check the document with CSS disabled and confirm that quotation and source relationships remain understandable.

questions.prompt: Which element is intended for a quotation presented as a separate block?
questions.explanation: blockquote represents an extended quotation that forms a block in the document.

questions.prompt: Which element marks the title of a creative work being referenced?
questions.explanation: The cite element identifies the title of a work; it is not a complete citation format.

questions.prompt: What does the cite attribute on blockquote provide?
options: Visible attribution text automatically shown by every browser
questions.explanation: The cite attribute provides a source URL but does not normally display a visible citation to readers.

questions.prompt: How should a short quotation inside a sentence usually be marked?
questions.explanation: q is the semantic element for a short inline quotation.

questions.prompt: A quotation is shortened. What should the author do?
options: Make the omission or adaptation clear and preserve accurate attribution
Present the shortened text as an exact unmodified quotation
Use CSS to hide the omitted words
questions.answer: Make the omission or adaptation clear and preserve accurate attribution
questions.explanation: Markup does not excuse misleading quotation practices; editorial changes should be disclosed.

questions.prompt: Which is the best way to make a source findable by readers?
options: Provide a visible source link or attribution
Rely only on the cite attribute
questions.answer: Provide a visible source link or attribution
questions.explanation: A visible link or attribution communicates the source to readers; cite metadata alone is not a visible citation.
